transcript: this new musical takes an eerie mystery and gives it kind of a Spring Awakening vibe based on the novel of the same name Picnic at Hanging Rock tells the story of 3 boarding school girls who mysteriously disappear while exploring the titular Hanging Rock in Australia I had actually seen a play adaptation of this story way back in high school and I found the story pretty captivating but I also left a little bit bemused I don't know if it was this new adaptation or just returning to the story now that I'm older but I had a deeper appreciation for what it was doing overall. I found it a lot more narratively and thematically satisfying. as for this musical specifically the score is very intricately written and has a lot of impressive harmonies and vocal arrangements which gives it an appropriately haunting quality but also with a bit of a dreamy, almost romantic undertone which does feel like it makes sense here because at least in this adaptation while the disappearance is extremely unsettling it also kind of speaks to this yearning for freedom that these young women feel in a world that restricts them and that's another way in which the Spring Awakening parallel kind of stuck out to me in addition to the aesthetic and certain elements of the score. As is often the case with new musicals though, I did struggle a bit with the book. apparently this musical has been performed in concert a few times throughout its development and you can kind of tell and I wondered if maybe they got a little too used to that format not because of the physical production but because the book book feels very skeletal like the spoken scenes are just kind of linking us to the next song which might be fine for a musical that's designed to be mostly sung through but it doesn't feel feel like that's quite the case here. it feels a bit awkwardly caught somewhere in between, with some plot and character arcs that feel rushed or undercooked. It only runs about 100 minutes not including the intermission and it's a rare case where I actually think a show might benefit from being longer to really take its time to let things unravel and let us sit with the ripple effects of the plot more meaningfully still though there's genuinely a lot to like about the musical from the story to the score to the performances so if you aren't able to catch this short run at the Greenwich House Theatre before it closes on January 17th it's worth keeping your eyes open for future iterations especially if it gets developed further
